name: Deep Focus
oneLiner: A slow heartbeat under a dark hum. Nothing asks for your attention.
rationale: Set at 72 beats a minute — a shade above a working pulse, quick enough to keep you awake but far too steady to chase. The drums are a two-part heartbeat rather than a pattern, and the bass sits on the same pulse, so there is a floor to lean on and no new event to notice. No melody at all: a tune is the one thing that reliably steals attention from what you are reading.

name: Open Plan
oneLiner: A wide, even wash sitting exactly where voices live.
rationale: Built to cover office chatter rather than compete with it: the texture holds a steady band of sound across the frequencies speech occupies, so a conversation two desks away stops resolving into words you can follow. Everything that could make you look up — drums, plucked notes, sudden entries — is switched off, and the slow drift in level stops your ears filing the whole thing away as machinery.

name: Glass Office
oneLiner: Cold daylight on hard surfaces, with a crystal figure turning over.
rationale: Lydian is the brightest of the everyday modes — the raised fourth is what film music reaches for when it wants sky — and against glass and crystal timbres it reads as daylight rather than evening. Held at 74 beats, just over a resting pulse, so it lifts without pushing; the little arpeggio repeats far more than it varies, which is what lets it become furniture inside a minute.

name: Long Read
oneLiner: A warm waltz with no tune in it — for reading, not for working to a beat.
rationale: Reading words and following a melody compete for the same machinery, so this one has no melodic line at all: a warm chord turning over in three-four, a grain of texture above it, and a marimba note every bar or so to mark time. At 66 beats it sits at a calm working pulse, and the repetition is set high enough that nothing new arrives to make you lose your place.

name: First Light
oneLiner: Marimba, hand drums and a light shuffle. The first hour of the day.
rationale: A morning ramp. 84 beats with a swing is well above resting but nowhere near exercise tempo, which is the band that lifts mood without dragging your heart rate up to meet it. The arrangement builds rather than starting at full pelt, so the first couple of minutes are sparse and the room fills as you settle — much easier to begin work to than something already busy.

name: Push
oneLiner: Ticking sixteenths and a bass locked to the kick. Head down, timer running.
rationale: The energising band — 112 beats, about the pace of a brisk walk — with almost everything repeated rather than varied, because propulsion helps a deadline and novelty does not. Dorian keeps it purposeful instead of cheerful, and the bass is pinned to the same slots as the kick so the rhythm section reads as one moving object you can ride instead of several things happening.

name: Sketchbook
oneLiner: Five beats to the bar, lydian, and a line that keeps changing its mind.
rationale: The opposite of the focus presets, on purpose: creative work benefits from a little unpredictability, so this one evolves rather than repeating, the flute line is allowed to lean outside the chord, and the five-beat bar never quite lets you settle. The tempo stays moderate at 88 — stimulating without hurrying you, which is where loose, associative thinking tends to live.

name: Night Shift
oneLiner: Warm, low and awake — for working while everyone else sleeps.
rationale: Late work needs to stay alert without turning harsh, so this holds 64 beats — just above rest, enough to keep you upright — and takes the brightness out of everything: a warm pad low in its register, a sub bass under it, and a tick you feel more than hear. Aeolian supplies the minor-key weight the hour asks for without tipping into anything mournful enough to notice.

name: Wind Down
oneLiner: Under a resting pulse, rocking in six-eight, everything falling away.
rationale: Music slower than a resting heartbeat tends to pull arousal down with it, which is why this one sits at 52 in a rocking six-eight. There is no percussion to march to and no melody to track — a choir pad and a wash that swell and recede, and little else — so it works as a full stop at the end of the day rather than as something to keep working to.

name: Breathe
oneLiner: One chord, swelling and releasing at about six breaths a minute.
rationale: Slow paced breathing is the quickest reliable way to bring arousal down, and this gives you something to follow: at 40 beats in six-eight each bar lasts around four and a half seconds, so a breath in and a breath out fills two bars, and the pad rises and falls on exactly that shape. Apart from an occasional grain of texture there is no pulse and no melodic line, because anything that arrives is one more thing to notice.
